# Why PHP Cannot Call Functions on Button Clicks Without a Form Submit

The core issue in your code stems from a fundamental misunderstanding of how HTML buttons and HTTP requests interact. You are attempting to execute server-side logic immediately upon clicking an element, but standard `<input type="button">` elements do not trigger any data submission to the server unless they are part of a form that is explicitly submitted.

In your `Calling.php` file, you have defined three inputs: two buttons labeled "B1" and "B2", and one submit button named "Submit1". The first two use `type="button"`. In HTML5 and earlier standards, an input with this type triggers a client-side JavaScript event called `click`, but it does **not** cause the browser to send a request to the server. Consequently, your `Called.php` file never receives any data when you click those buttons.

The third button uses `type="Submit"` (which is technically deprecated in favor of `type="submit"`). This element acts as the trigger for the form's default action. When clicked, it packages the current form data and sends an HTTP request to the `action` attribute defined on the `<form>` tag. In your example, that target is `Called.php` with the method set to `get`.

This architectural difference explains why only the "Submit" button works. Clicking "B1" or "B2" simply changes focus or runs a local script if one were attached via JavaScript; it does not invoke PHP functions in `Called.php`. The server remains unaware that the user clicked anything until the form is submitted.

### Correcting the Logic in `Called.php`

Your current check for the buttons uses `isset($_GET("Submit1"))` and similar patterns. There are two distinct problems here. First, `isset()` checks for array key existence; it does not take a string argument directly without an array context. The correct syntax is `isset($_GET['key'])`. Second, relying on `$_GET` to detect button clicks that never submit data will always fail.

To make the buttons in `Calling.php` functional within this specific architecture, you must change their type to `submit`:

```html
<input type="submit" name="B1" value="B1">
<input type="submit" name="B2" value="B2">
```

With this change, clicking "B1" will indeed populate the `$_GET['B1']` variable in `Called.php`. Your existing PHP logic:

```php
if(isset($_GET["B1"]))
{
    echo("<script>location.href = 'http://google.com/';</script>");
    exit();
} 
```

will then work as intended, provided the syntax for `isset` is corrected to use array brackets.

### The Blinking Effect and Redirects

You mentioned that the page blinks but does not redirect when clicking "B1" or "B2". This behavior occurs because the browser waits for the form submission to complete before loading a new URL. When you click a `type="button"` (or even `type="submit"`), the browser processes the event, sends the request, and then waits for the response from the server.

In your current code, `Called.php` echoes a script tag or a meta refresh tag. The browser renders this content immediately as part of the HTML document. Because the page is not empty when it loads, the redirection script executes after the page has already rendered, causing that brief flash or "blink."

A cleaner approach for redirects is to ensure the response body is empty until the redirect logic runs. While your current method works, frameworks like Laravel handle this more robustly using `redirect()` helpers which automatically clear the output buffer and issue the 302 status code cleanly. If you are moving beyond vanilla PHP, integrating a framework like [https://laravelcompany.com](https://laravelcompany.com) can help manage these state transitions without relying on raw HTML meta tags or inline script tags that cause flickering.

### Security and Best Practices

Relying solely on `$_GET` variables to determine flow is fragile. If you are building a larger application, consider moving this logic into a controller pattern where routes map specific URLs to actions. This prevents direct manipulation of parameters via the URL bar (e.g., typing `Calling.php?B1=1`) and provides better separation of concerns.

Finally, be aware that using `<meta http-equiv='refresh'>` is often considered an anti-pattern in modern development because it executes after the DOM is loaded and can be intercepted by JavaScript. Using JavaScript's `window.location.href` or a proper 302 redirect from the server is generally preferred for performance and clarity.
